title: Muhammad Ali and the Khedivate
subtitle: 1798–1900 · The Founding of a Modern State, the Suez Canal, the Debt, and the British Occupation

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Muhammad Ali's founding of a modern state and dynasty, the Khedives, the ʿUrabi revolt, and the British occupation of 1882

entries.label: The struggle for power, 1801–1805
entries.hint: After the French withdrawal in 1801, Egypt was fought over by Ottoman troops, the surviving Mamluk beys, and the Albanian irregulars of the sultan's contingent. Muhammad Ali, an Albanian officer, manoeuvred among them, courted the Cairo populace and the ulama, and in 1805 the notables — led by the naqib al-ashraf 'Umar Makram — deposed the Ottoman governor and demanded that the Porte confirm Muhammad Ali as wali. It did.
entries.note: Al-Jabarti, 'Aja'ib al-athar. Afaf Lutfi al-Sayyid Marsot, Egypt in the Reign of Muhammad Ali (1984) pp.24–56; Khaled Fahmy, Mehmed Ali: From Ottoman Governor to Ruler of Egypt (2009) pp.1–30.

entries.label: Muhammad Ali, the founder
entries.hint: In four decades Muhammad Ali built a new kind of Egyptian state: a conscript peasant army trained on the European model, a navy, a state monopoly over agriculture and trade, long-staple cotton as an export crop, factories and arsenals, schools and printing, a land survey. He used it to conquer the Sudan and Arabia, fight in Greece, and twice invade Syria, until in 1841 the European powers forced him to give up his conquests in return for a hereditary governorship for his family.
entries.note: Khaled Fahmy, All the Pasha's Men: Mehmed Ali, His Army and the Making of Modern Egypt (1997); Marsot, Egypt in the Reign of Muhammad Ali (1984).

entries.label: Ibrahim Pasha, the general
entries.hint: Muhammad Ali's eldest son commanded almost every campaign: the destruction of the Saudi state in Arabia, the war in the Greek Morea, and the conquest of Syria in 1831–33, which he then governed and defended, winning the crushing victory of Nezib in 1839. He identified with Egypt more than his Ottoman-minded father and was popular with the troops. He held the governorship for a few months in 1848 while Muhammad Ali sank into senility, and died before him.
entries.note: Fahmy, All the Pasha's Men (1997). Ibrahim's Syrian government: Asad Rustum, The Royal Archives of Egypt and the Disturbances in Palestine, 1834 (1938).

entries.label: Abbas I
entries.hint: Muhammad Ali's grandson Abbas I is remembered — largely through hostile later accounts — as a reactionary who dismissed European advisers, shut schools and factories, and withdrew into a fortified palace in the desert. He kept Egypt out of the Ottoman-Russian tensions, resisted French pressure for a Suez canal, and granted a British company the concession for the first Egyptian railway. He was murdered by two of his own servants in 1854.
entries.note: F. Robert Hunter, Egypt under the Khedives 1805–1879: From Household Government to Modern Bureaucracy (1984) pp.36–47. The rehabilitating view: Marsot, A History of Egypt (2007).

entries.label: Saʿid
entries.hint: Saʿid, a son of Muhammad Ali educated in France and a friend of Ferdinand de Lesseps, granted the concession for the Suez Canal in 1854 and 1856 — with clauses committing Egypt to supply forced labour and buy most of the shares. He completed the Alexandria–Cairo railway, began dismantling his father's monopolies, and issued the land law of 1858 that moved Egypt toward private property in land. He took the first of the foreign loans that would end in bankruptcy.
entries.note: Hunter, Egypt under the Khedives (1984) pp.48–60; David Landes, Bankers and Pashas: International Finance and Economic Imperialism in Egypt (1958).

entries.label: Ismaʿil — the moderniser and the bankrupt
entries.hint: Ismaʿil rode the cotton boom of the American Civil War, opened the Suez Canal in 1869 with a European festival, rebuilt central Cairo on Paris lines, bought the hereditary title Khedive and the right of primogeniture from the Sultan, expanded the courts, schools and the railway network, and pushed Egyptian rule to the Great Lakes. He also borrowed on ruinous terms. By 1876 Egypt was bankrupt, its finances under an Anglo-French commission and 'Dual Control'; in 1879 the Sultan deposed him at European insistence.
entries.note: Hunter, Egypt under the Khedives (1984); Landes, Bankers and Pashas (1958); Alexander Schölch, Ägypten den Ägyptern! (1972, Eng. Egypt for the Egyptians!, 1981).

entries.label: Tawfiq
entries.hint: Tawfiq was placed on the throne by the powers when his father was deposed. His reign was consumed by the ʿUrabi crisis: pressed between the army and the nationalists on one side and the European controllers on the other, he sided with the British, fled Cairo for Alexandria under their protection during the 1882 fighting, and was restored by their army. He reigned for another decade as a figurehead under Lord Cromer.
entries.note: Schölch, Egypt for the Egyptians! (1981); Juan Cole, Colonialism and Revolution in the Middle East (1993). Wilfrid Scawen Blunt, Secret History of the English Occupation of Egypt (1907).

entries.label: Abbas II Hilmi
entries.hint: Abbas II came to the throne at seventeen and at once tried to assert himself against Cromer — dismissing a British-favoured minister in 1893, criticising the Egyptian army's British officers in 1894. Cromer forced him to back down each time. The young Khedive then gave quiet encouragement to the emerging nationalist press and to Mustafa Kamil's movement, while accommodating the occupation in public — a stance that satisfied no one.
entries.note: Robert Tignor, Modernization and British Colonial Rule in Egypt 1882–1914 (1966); Roger Owen, Lord Cromer: Victorian Imperialist, Edwardian Proconsul (2004) pp.246–72.

entries.label: The ʿUrabi movement
entries.hint: Egyptian-born army officers, led by Colonel Ahmad ʿUrabi and protesting the promotion bar against non-Turco-Circassians and the budget cuts demanded by the foreign controllers, allied with the Chamber of Delegates, big landowners and the ulama in a movement summed up as 'Egypt for the Egyptians'. In September 1881 an armed demonstration forced Tawfiq to change the government; by February 1882 a nationalist ministry held office with ʿUrabi as minister of war. Britain and France read it as a threat to the debt and the canal.
entries.note: Juan Cole, Colonialism and Revolution in the Middle East: Social and Cultural Origins of Egypt's 'Urabi Movement (1993); Schölch, Egypt for the Egyptians! (1981).

entries.label: The occupation and Lord Cromer
entries.hint: After Tel el-Kebir a British army stayed 'temporarily' — for seventy years. From 1883 the Consul-General, Sir Evelyn Baring, later Lord Cromer, was the real ruler, governing through Egyptian ministers shadowed by British 'advisers' whose word was final. His priorities were servicing the debt and reforming the irrigation; his neglect of Egyptian education and of promoting Egyptians was deliberate and lasting. The arrangement — occupation without annexation — was called the 'Veiled Protectorate'.
entries.note: Roger Owen, Lord Cromer (2004); Robert Tignor, Modernization and British Colonial Rule in Egypt 1882–1914 (1966). Cromer's own apologia: Modern Egypt (1908).

entries.label: The Egyptian Sudan
entries.hint: Muhammad Ali's armies conquered Nubia, Sennar and Kordofan in 1820–21, and Khartoum was founded at the junction of the Niles in 1830 as the capital of an Egyptian colony run for slaves, ivory and gold. Ismaʿil pushed it far south — Gordon governed the Equatorial province and Bahr al-Ghazal, Darfur was annexed in 1874 — and layered a European-officered administration and an anti-slave-trade campaign onto a regime the Sudanese experienced as harsh, extractive alien rule.
entries.note: P.M. Holt & M.W. Daly, A History of the Sudan (6th ed. 2011) chs. 4–8; Richard Hill, Egypt in the Sudan 1820–1881 (1959); Douglas Johnson (ed.), Sudan (2 vols, 1998) for Gordon and the equatorial provinces.

entries.label: The Mahdiyya
entries.hint: In 1881 Muhammad Ahmad, a Dongola boat-builder's son and Sufi shaykh, proclaimed himself the Mahdi, the divinely guided renewer, and raised a revolt against Egyptian rule and its taxes. His armies destroyed the Egyptian forces sent against them, culminating in the annihilation of Hicks Pasha's column in 1883; Khartoum fell in January 1885. The Mahdi died months later, and his successor the Khalifa Abdullahi ruled an independent Islamic Sudanese state from Omdurman for thirteen years.
entries.note: P.M. Holt, The Mahdist State in the Sudan 1881–1898 (2nd ed. 1970); Holt & Daly, A History of the Sudan, chs. 9–11.

entries.label: The reconquest and the Condominium
entries.hint: An Anglo-Egyptian army under Sir Herbert Kitchener advanced up the Nile from 1896, building a desert railway as it went, and on 2 September 1898 shattered the Khalifa's army outside Omdurman with artillery and machine-guns. Days later a small French expedition under Marchand was found holding the fort at Fashoda on the Upper Nile; a diplomatic confrontation ended in French withdrawal. The Condominium agreement of January 1899 gave Egypt nominal co-sovereignty over a Sudan run in fact by Britain.
entries.note: Holt & Daly, A History of the Sudan, ch. 12; Douglas Johnson, 'The Death of Gordon: A Victorian Myth', Journal of Imperial and Commonwealth History 10 (1982); Darrell Bates, The Fashoda Incident of 1898 (1984).

entries.label: The Chamber of Delegates and the constitutional experiment
entries.hint: Ismaʿil created a Chamber of Delegates in 1866, largely of village headmen and landowners, meant to be a rubber stamp. In the 1876–1879 crisis it turned assertive, demanding control of the budget and backing the 'National' ministry against the European controllers; in 1882 the ʿUrabists drafted a constitution and the Chamber claimed real legislative power. Britain suspended it after the occupation, replacing it with the toothless Legislative Council and General Assembly of 1883 — but the idea of an Egyptian parliament was now planted.
entries.note: Schölch, Egypt for the Egyptians! (1981) pp.153–83; Jacob Landau, Parliaments and Parties in Egypt (1953); Nathan Brown, 'Who Abolished Corvée Labour in Egypt and Why?', Past & Present 144 (1994) for the Chamber's later role.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The massacre of the Mamluks, the wars in Arabia, the Sudan, Greece and Syria, ʿUrabi and Tel el-Kebir, and the Mahdist wars

entries.group: The End of the French Occupation
entries.label: The expulsion of the French
entries.hint: A British expeditionary force under Sir Ralph Abercromby landed at Aboukir in March 1801, beat the French near Alexandria — Abercromby was mortally wounded — and, with an Ottoman army advancing from Syria, closed on Cairo. The isolated French garrison, its fleet long gone, capitulated: the army was repatriated on British ships, taking its scientific collections but surrendering, after a dispute, the Rosetta Stone. Three years of occupation had shattered the old order without replacing it.
entries.note: Piers Mackesy, British Victory in Egypt, 1801 (1995). Al-Jabarti's account of the end of the occupation. The Rosetta Stone dispute: the Capitulation of Alexandria, article 16.

entries.label: The massacre of the Mamluks
entries.hint: On 1 March 1811, at a banquet in the Citadel marking his son's departure for Arabia, Muhammad Ali had the Mamluk beys and their retinues shot down in the walled passage between the gates as they rode out — several hundred men in minutes. Hunting parties killed hundreds more across the country in the following weeks. The Mamluk military caste that had dominated Egypt for five and a half centuries was destroyed, and with it the last organised check on the new ruler.
entries.note: Al-Jabarti, 'Aja'ib al-athar. Marsot, Egypt in the Reign of Muhammad Ali (1984) pp.60–61; the eyewitness accounts collected in Henry Dodwell, The Founder of Modern Egypt (1931).

entries.label: The war against the Saudis in Arabia
entries.hint: At the Ottoman sultan's request, Muhammad Ali sent an army to retake the Holy Cities from the first Saudi state and the Wahhabi movement. His son Tusun recovered Mecca and Medina by 1813; Ibrahim then drove into Najd and, after a months-long siege, took and demolished the Saudi capital Diriyah in 1818, sending the captured imam Abdullah to Istanbul to be beheaded. The first Saudi state was extinguished, and Egypt held western Arabia for a generation.
entries.note: Fahmy, All the Pasha's Men (1997) pp.38–75. The Saudi side: R. Bayly Winder, Saudi Arabia in the Nineteenth Century (1965); see the Arabia folios.

entries.label: The conquest of the Sudan
entries.hint: Muhammad Ali sent expeditions south to seize the Sudan for its supposed gold and, above all, for slaves to fill his new conscript army. The armies of his son Ismaʿil Kamil and his son-in-law the Daftardar overran Nubia, the Funj sultanate of Sennar and Kordofan against uneven resistance. When the local ruler of Shendi burned Ismaʿil Kamil alive in his tent in 1822, the Daftardar's reprisal killed thousands. The captured Sudanese slave-soldiers died in droves of disease before the army was rebuilt on Egyptian conscripts.
entries.note: Richard Hill, Egypt in the Sudan 1820–1881 (1959); Fahmy, All the Pasha's Men (1997) pp.87–96; Holt & Daly, A History of the Sudan, ch. 4.

entries.label: The Greek war and Navarino
entries.hint: The Ottomans called in the Egyptian fleet and Ibrahim's army to crush the Greek revolt, and by 1826 he had reconquered most of the Morea with a ruthlessness that horrified European opinion. On 20 October 1827 a combined British, French and Russian fleet destroyed the anchored Egyptian-Ottoman navy at Navarino, and by 1828 a French landing forced the Egyptians out of Greece. Muhammad Ali had lost his fleet, his best troops and years of revenue in someone else's war.
entries.note: C.M. Woodhouse, The Battle of Navarino (1965); Fahmy, All the Pasha's Men (1997) pp.53–75. The Greek dimension: Douglas Dakin, The Greek Struggle for Independence (1973).

entries.label: The Syrian wars and the crisis of 1840
entries.hint: Denied Syria as a reward for Greece, Muhammad Ali took it by force. Ibrahim stormed Acre, beat the Ottoman army at Konya in 1832, and by 1833 held Syria, Palestine and Cilicia. His conscription and taxes there sparked revolts he suppressed brutally. When war resumed in 1839 he won again at Nezib and the Ottoman fleet defected to him — but Britain, Austria, Russia and Prussia intervened, bombarded Beirut and Acre, and imposed the Treaty of London: Egypt evacuated Syria and Arabia and cut its army, in return for the hereditary governorship it had wanted all along.
entries.note: Fahmy, All the Pasha's Men (1997) pp.76–111; Marsot, Egypt in the Reign of Muhammad Ali (1984). The Eastern Crisis: M.S. Anderson, The Eastern Question 1774–1923 (1966).

entries.label: Alexandria and Tel el-Kebir
entries.hint: After riots in Alexandria in June 1882 in which dozens of Europeans and many Egyptians died, the British fleet bombarded the city's forts on 11 July; France, which had backed the naval demonstration, drew back and left Britain to act alone. A British army landed at Ismailia on the canal and, before dawn on 13 September, overran ʿUrabi's entrenched position at Tel el-Kebir in twenty minutes. ʿUrabi surrendered, was tried for rebellion, and exiled to Ceylon. The occupation had begun.
entries.note: Schölch, Egypt for the Egyptians! (1981) pp.235–319; Donald Featherstone, Tel el-Kebir 1882 (1993). The bombardment: A.B. Wilson and the naval records.

entries.label: The fall of Khartoum
entries.hint: With the Egyptian army broken, the British-run government in Cairo decided to abandon the Sudan and sent General Charles Gordon to organise the evacuation. Gordon instead dug in at Khartoum, which the Mahdi's forces besieged from March 1884. A British relief column moving up the Nile was still two days away when the city fell on 26 January 1885 and Gordon was killed. Egypt withdrew from the Sudan entirely, and Gordon's death became a lasting grievance in British politics.
entries.note: Holt, The Mahdist State in the Sudan (1970); Douglas Johnson, 'The Death of Gordon: A Victorian Myth' (1982). The relief expedition: Adrian Preston (ed.), In Relief of Gordon (1967).

entries.label: Omdurman and Fashoda
entries.hint: On 2 September 1898 Kitchener's Anglo-Egyptian army met the Khalifa's forces outside Omdurman. Massed rifle fire, artillery and Maxim guns killed around eleven thousand Sudanese for the loss of about fifty of their own; Winston Churchill, present with the cavalry, called it 'the most signal triumph ever gained by the arms of science over barbarians'. Three weeks later Kitchener sailed on to Fashoda to face down a French flag-planting expedition, and the whole Nile fell under British control.
entries.note: Winston Churchill, The River War (1899). Holt & Daly, A History of the Sudan, ch. 12; Darrell Bates, The Fashoda Incident of 1898 (1984).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The conscript army, the state monopolies, the cadastre and private property in land, the Mixed Courts, and Cromer's administration

entries.label: The conscript army
entries.hint: When his Sudanese slave-soldiers died of disease, Muhammad Ali did the unthinkable and conscripted the Egyptian peasantry — men seized from the fields, branded, marched in chains to camps, and drilled on the European model by the French officer Colonel Sèves (Suleiman Pasha). The army reached around 130,000 men and was the engine and template of the whole reform: it drove the demand for conscription bureaux, medical schools, factories, veterinary science and a survey. It also cost Egypt a generation of rural labour and provoked flight, self-mutilation and revolt.
entries.note: Khaled Fahmy, All the Pasha's Men: Mehmed Ali, His Army and the Making of Modern Egypt (1997) — the definitive study.

entries.label: The monopoly state and the modern bureaucracy
entries.hint: Muhammad Ali made the government the sole buyer of every crop at a fixed low price and the sole exporter at the world price, ran the factories and the trade, and staffed a growing set of ministries (dawawin) with salaried officials. His successors, forced to retrench and pressed by European free-traders, dismantled the monopolies over the 1840s–60s. What remained was a permanent salaried bureaucracy — Egypt had moved, in F. Robert Hunter's phrase, 'from household government to modern bureaucracy'.
entries.note: F. Robert Hunter, Egypt under the Khedives 1805–1879: From Household Government to Modern Bureaucracy (1984). The monopolies: Marsot, Egypt in the Reign of Muhammad Ali (1984); Roger Owen, The Middle East in the World Economy 1800–1914 (1981).

entries.label: The cadastre and private property in land
entries.hint: Muhammad Ali confiscated the tax-farms and much waqf revenue and had the land surveyed and registered. Over the century a series of laws — Saʿid's of 1858, the Muqabala of 1871, the Law of Liquidation of 1880 — turned agricultural land into heritable, saleable, mortgageable near-freehold property. The result was a landed elite: the royal family, the Turco-Circassian officers, and increasingly Egyptian village notables, holding large estates worked as 'izbas by resident tenant-labourers, alongside a mass of smallholders and landless.
entries.note: Kenneth Cuno, The Pasha's Peasants: Land, Society, and Economy in Lower Egypt 1740–1858 (1992); Gabriel Baer, A History of Landownership in Modern Egypt 1800–1950 (1962); Alan Richards, Egypt's Agricultural Development 1800–1980 (1982).

entries.label: The Mixed Courts and the capitulations
entries.hint: Foreign residents claimed exemption from Egyptian courts and taxes under the Ottoman capitulations, and by the 1870s the privileges were a byword for abuse — foreigners lending at usury, evading tax, and dragging the government before their own consuls. Nubar Pasha's reform created the Mixed Courts in 1876, staffed by Egyptian and foreign judges and applying French-based codes to any case involving a foreigner. The Native Courts followed in 1883. The legal order was modern in form but layered and unequal.
entries.note: Nathan Brown, 'The Precarious Life and Slow Death of the Mixed Courts of Egypt', IJMES 25 (1993); Jasper Yeates Brinton, The Mixed Courts of Egypt (1930). The capitulations: Byron Cannon, Politics of Law and the Courts in Nineteenth-Century Egypt (1988).

entries.label: The debt and the Caisse de la Dette
entries.hint: Between 1862 and 1873 Egypt raised loan after loan on the London and Paris markets at effective rates of 12 to 25 per cent, the money going into the canal, the railways, Ismaʿil's palaces and wars, and the servicing of earlier loans. In 1875 the Suez Canal shares were sold to Britain; in 1876 Egypt's revenues were placed under the Caisse de la Dette Publique, with foreign commissioners taking the customs and other taxes off the top; and the Law of Liquidation of 1880 fixed about two-thirds of state revenue for the bondholders.
entries.note: David Landes, Bankers and Pashas: International Finance and Economic Imperialism in Egypt (1958) — the classic account. Roger Owen, The Middle East in the World Economy (1981) pp.122–52.

entries.label: The Veiled Protectorate
entries.hint: Britain governed occupied Egypt without annexing it. Egyptian ministers held office, but in each department a British 'adviser' had the final word, and the Financial Adviser held a formal veto over all spending; the Consul-General, Lord Cromer, outranked them all. Cromer put the money into debt service and irrigation and kept it away from schools, held Egyptians out of the higher administration, and restricted political life — a system its defenders called reform and its critics called colonial rule behind a curtain.
entries.note: Robert Tignor, Modernization and British Colonial Rule in Egypt 1882–1914 (1966); Roger Owen, Lord Cromer (2004). The critique: A.G. Hopkins, 'The Victorians and Africa: A Reconsideration of the Occupation of Egypt, 1882', Journal of African History 27 (1986).

entries.label: The corvée, the courbash and the fellah
entries.hint: The reforming state ran on forced labour and the whip. The corvée mobilised hundreds of thousands of peasants each year for unpaid work clearing the canals and building the public works — including, until 1863, most of the digging of the Suez Canal itself. The courbash, the hippopotamus-hide lash, was standard in tax collection and conscription. British administrators, partly from principle and partly to free labour for the cotton estates, cut back the state corvée from 1884 and abolished it for public works by 1892.
entries.note: Nathan Brown, 'Who Abolished Corvée Labour in Egypt and Why?', Past & Present 144 (1994); Zachary Lockman, 'Notes on Egyptian Workers' History', International Labor and Working-Class History 34 (1988). The canal corvée: John Marlowe, The Making of the Suez Canal (1964).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Al-Azhar and its reform, Muhammad ʿAbduh and Islamic modernism, the Coptic reform movement, and the Sufi orders under the state

entries.label: al-Azhar and the ulama between old and new
entries.hint: Al-Azhar remained the heart of Islamic learning, but the ulama's political weight fell away fast: the shaykhs who had made Muhammad Ali wali in 1805 saw their leader 'Umar Makram exiled in 1809, and the state went on to seize much of the waqf that funded their independence. The shaykh al-Azhar became a government appointment; the curriculum and administration were repeatedly put up for reform; and the ulama slid from being the notables of Egypt to being one interest group among several.
entries.note: Afaf Lutfi al-Sayyid Marsot, 'The Ulama of Cairo in the Eighteenth and Nineteenth Centuries', in Keddie (ed.), Scholars, Saints, and Sufis (1972); Daniel Crecelius, 'Nonideological Responses of the Egyptian Ulama to Modernization', ibid.

entries.label: Al-Afghani, ʿAbduh and Islamic modernism
entries.hint: Jamal al-Din al-Afghani taught a circle of young Egyptians in the 1870s that Islam must be revived and defended against European power by adopting reason, science and constitutional politics. His disciple Muhammad ʿAbduh — exiled after the ʿUrabi revolt, then rehabilitated and made Grand Mufti of Egypt in 1899 — argued that true Islam was fully compatible with modern thought and pressed for reform of al-Azhar and of the sharia courts. Through his student Rashid Rida's journal al-Manar the movement shaped Muslim reform across the world.
entries.note: Albert Hourani, Arabic Thought in the Liberal Age 1798–1939 (1962) chs. 5–6; Nikki Keddie, Sayyid Jamal ad-Din 'al-Afghani' (1972); Malcolm Kerr, Islamic Reform (1966).

entries.label: The Coptic reform movement and the missions
entries.hint: Patriarch Cyril IV, 'the father of reform', founded Coptic schools — including one for girls — a press and a library, and curbed clerical abuses before his early death in 1861. American Presbyterian missionaries, arriving in 1854 and working mainly among Copts, built a network of schools and eventually an Evangelical Coptic Church. A reforming Coptic laity, enriched by the century's opportunities, pressed for a say in church affairs, winning a Community Council in 1874 that then feuded for decades with the hierarchy over the endowments.
entries.note: B.L. Carter, The Copts in Egyptian Politics 1918–1952 (1986) for the background; Paul Sedra, From Mission to Modernity: Evangelicals, Reformers and Education in Nineteenth-Century Egypt (2011).

entries.label: The Sufi orders under the state
entries.hint: Popular Sufism remained a mass institution — the mawlids of Tanta and Cairo still drew vast crowds — but it was brought under state supervision. The Bakri family, and later the Sadat, held a government-recognised headship over all the orders, formalised by decree in 1881 and 1895 into the 'Council of Sufi Orders', which registered the tariqas, licensed shaykhs and regulated the festivals. Modernists and Islamic reformers increasingly attacked the whole culture of the saints as superstition.
entries.note: F. de Jong, Turuq and Turuq-Linked Institutions in Nineteenth Century Egypt: A Historical Study in Organizational Dimensions of Islamic Mysticism (1978).

entries.label: The Jewish community and the Geniza
entries.hint: The Jewish community grew and diversified through the century — Sephardi and Italian families, later Ashkenazi immigrants, alongside the old Egyptian and Karaite communities — and became prominent in finance, the Mixed Courts and the professions in Cairo and Alexandria. It was also in this century that Western scholars realised what lay in the storeroom of the medieval Ben Ezra synagogue: Solomon Schechter carried some 190,000 fragments of the Cairo Geniza to Cambridge in 1896–97, opening a thousand years of Mediterranean Jewish life to study.
entries.note: Jacob Landau, Jews in Nineteenth-Century Egypt (1969). The Geniza: Stefan Reif, A Jewish Archive from Old Cairo (2000); Adina Hoffman & Peter Cole, Sacred Trash (2011).

entries.label: Religion, the state and national identity
entries.hint: The century opened a question Egypt is still arguing: what kind of community is it? An Ottoman-Muslim province, a part of the Arab or Islamic world, or a territorial nation of Egyptians — Muslim and Copt together — defined by the Nile and a shared history? The ʿUrabi movement's 'Egypt for the Egyptians' and the early nationalist press leaned toward the last; ʿAbduh's Islamic reform and, later, Mustafa Kamil's Ottoman-tinged nationalism offered others. The Coptic place in the answer was contested from the start.
entries.note: Israel Gershoni & James Jankowski, Egypt, Islam, and the Arabs: The Search for Egyptian Nationhood 1900–1930 (1986), with its 19th-century prologue; Juan Cole, Colonialism and Revolution in the Middle East (1993).

categories.subtitle: Muhammad Ali and Ismaʿil, Rifaʿa al-Tahtawi, Ahmad ʿUrabi, and the fellah under the corvée and the whip
